acrid

AK-rid · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Acrid is having a harsh, bitter smell or taste, especially from burning or chemicals.

An acrid cloud hung over the chemistry lab after the beaker of sulfur was accidentally overheated.

Example

The firefighters described an acrid stench of melted plastic that clung to their gear for days after the warehouse fire.

The smell wasn't mild or pleasant -- it was harsh and bitter enough to linger unpleasantly, exactly what acrid describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

harsh: Harsh is the broad word for anything roughly unpleasant to the senses — harsh light, harsh words, a harsh winter wind. Acrid is far narrower: a harsh, stinging smell or taste, nearly always from smoke or chemicals. Every acrid fume is harsh, but most harsh things are not acrid.

rank: Rank describes a smell that is strong, stale, and unwashed — old gym gear, a damp locker room. Acrid points instead at the sharp chemical bite of smoke and fumes. Rank air makes you wrinkle your nose; acrid air makes your eyes water and your throat sting.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fragrant: having a pleasant smell

sweet: pleasant tasting or smelling

Where it sits · how harsh the smell or taste — sour → acrid → putrid

sour vs. acrid: Something sour has a sharp, unpleasant taste, but nowhere near as harsh as an acrid one.

putrid vs. acrid: Something putrid is foully rotten-smelling, an even more extreme and disgusting smell than merely acrid.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — acr-

Root — acr-: sharp, bitter (from Latin acer, acris, 'sharp')

Suffix — -id

Suffix — -id: having the quality of (Latin -idus)

Put it together

Put it together: Acrid comes from Latin acer, 'sharp, bitter': acr- ('sharp, bitter') + -id ('having the quality of'). The same root gives us acrimony -- bitterness in speech or manner, the same harshness applied to how people treat each other instead of how something smells.

Use the root in a new word: acrimony

Use the root in a new word: acrimony: The mediator was brought in to deal with the acrimony between the two business partners.

Root Check

Word Choice

Acrid almost always carries a negative charge, especially for smoke, chemicals, or fumes -- unlike pungent, which can describe a strong smell that isn't necessarily unpleasant.
